methods.label: Count crossings through three sections
methods.explanation:
The restriction on repeating segments also prevents repeating vertices. Each internal vertex has at most three incident segments, whereas arriving and departing twice would require four different segments. Returning to \(A\) would likewise leave no unused segment for departing again.

[Figure 1](figures/2012_AMC_10B_Q25_question_fig1.svg)

Read the horizontal-arrow columns from left to right. The four columns containing only rightward arrows have \(2,4,4,2\) arrows. They separate the lattice into three sections. Once the bug crosses one of these columns, it cannot return across it. Thus we can count paths through one section at a time.

Within each section, the sloping segments form a left zigzag chain and a right zigzag chain, connected by horizontal arrows. Call these chains the two rails. There is exactly one leftward arrow, in the central row. A route through the section must therefore cross between the rails either once rightward, or three times in the order rightward, leftward, rightward. There cannot be more crossings because the leftward arrow can be used only once. Once the entrance, exit, and horizontal crossings are specified, the connecting routes along the rails are unique.

For three crossings, the two rightward arrows must lie on opposite sides of the central row. To see why, suppose both were above it. If the first arrow is farther from the central row, the journey down the right rail passes the vertex needed for the final crossing. If the last arrow is farther away, the journey up the left rail revisits the vertex of the first crossing. Both violate the no-repeated-vertex observation. The same argument applies below the central row.

Also, the entrance must be on the same side of the central row as the first rightward arrow, and the exit on the same side as the last. Otherwise a connecting rail journey repeats a vertex. Conversely, these side conditions make the three crossings and their connecting rail segments distinct, so every such choice is valid.

Suppose each entrance to a section has \(w\) paths reaching it. We count paths to one fixed exit.

In the first, widening section, there are two entrances and two rightward arrows. A single crossing contributes \(2\cdot2w=4w\). For three crossings, the fixed exit determines the side of the last arrow. There is one entrance, one first arrow, and one last arrow on the required sides, contributing \(w\). Thus each of the four exits receives \(5w\) paths.

In the middle section, there are four entrances and four rightward arrows. Single crossings contribute \(4\cdot4w=16w\). For three crossings, there are two entrances on the required side, two choices of the first arrow, and two choices of the last arrow, contributing \(2\cdot2\cdot2w=8w\). Each of its four exits therefore receives \(24w\) paths.

In the final, narrowing section, single crossings contribute \(4\cdot2w=8w\). Three crossings contribute \(2\cdot1\cdot1w=2w\), so each of its two exits receives \(10w\) paths.

There is one initial route from \(A\) to each of the first two entrances. Consequently, the counts per exit progress as
\[
1\longrightarrow5\longrightarrow24\cdot5=120
\longrightarrow10\cdot120=1200.
\]
Each final exit has one continuation to \(B\). Our cases are exhaustive, and each route has a unique entrance and crossing sequence in every section, so no route is counted twice. The total is
\[
1200+1200=\boxed{2400},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).

candidate.annotationRationale: The task requires an exhaustive count of restricted routes, so combined addition and multiplication is the task-level target. The written method additionally uses state recursion: one-way separators make the section and entrance vertex sufficient information for continuing the count. Graph degrees justify excluding repeated vertices, while the addition and multiplication principles support the local cases. These annotations do not establish learner mastery.

review.mathematicalCheck: The displayed rails allow either one rightward crossing or rightward-leftward-rightward crossings. The stated opposite-side conditions exactly prevent repeated vertices. The section counts are 5w, 24w, and 10w per exit, giving 2·5·24·10 = 2400 without omission or duplication.
